Synthetic Data: the Temporal Case

Source: vignettes/synthetic-data-temporal.Rmd
synthetic-data-temporal.Rmd

Every detector needs examples — positives to prove recall, near-misses to prove precision (see vignette("autotype-framework")). For most families those examples are hand-collected. But some types can be synthesized: generated in unlimited quantity, correctly labelled, for free. The temporal family is the clearest case, and it makes a good template for deciding when synthesis is worth it elsewhere.

Why temporal is the ideal case

A date or time has two properties that make it cheap to synthesize:

  1. One canonical value. “The 15th of March, 2016” is a single point in time — an R Date or POSIXct — no matter how it is written.
  2. Deterministic, enumerable rendering. That one value can be written in a known, finite set of surface formats, and format() renders any of them exactly. There is no ambiguity and no external resource required.

The temporal family is also the one with the most surface forms: the shipped examples in data-raw/datatypes/datetime.R cover seventeen representations of the same underlying thing —

iso_date · iso_datetime · us_date · us_datetime · abbr_month_date · long_date
month_year · yyyymm · month_day · clock_time · date_range · hijri_date · date
quarter · fiscal_year · day_of_week · month_of_year

— which is exactly why hand-curating them is tedious and why generating them pays off. The flexible date detector already carries the format vocabulary: see .date_formats_for() in R/dt-date-flex.R, which assembles the strftime patterns (%Y-%m-%d, %m/%d/%y, %B %d, %Y, …) the detector tries.

Generating positives

Sample canonical values once, then render each representation from them. Every rendered column is correctly labelled by construction.

set.seed(514)
days <- as.Date("1970-01-01") + sample(0:20000, 200)   # 200 random dates

# one strftime pattern per representation -> one labelled synthetic column each
renderings <- list(
  iso_date        = "%Y-%m-%d",
  us_date         = "%m/%d/%Y",
  abbr_month_date = "%d-%b-%Y",
  long_date       = "%A, %B %d, %Y",
  month_year      = "%B %Y",
  yyyymm          = "%Y%m",
  day_of_week     = "%A"
)
synthetic <- lapply(renderings, function(fmt) format(days, fmt))

str(synthetic$iso_date)   #> "1997-05-19" "2031-11-02" ...
str(synthetic$long_date)  #> "Monday, May 19, 1997" ...

Because the label is the key of renderings, a few lines produce hundreds of columns across every temporal representation — the positives a detector or the router needs, with no hand-labelling.

Generating hard negatives for free

Synthesis also hands you negatives that hand-curation cannot easily produce:

  • Out-of-range but well-formed: render month 13 or day 32 to test that a detector enforces ranges, not just the shape ("2016-13-05").
  • Format collisions: %m/%d/%Y vs %d/%m/%Y (“03/04/2016”) are the same string for different dates — a built-in ambiguity case.
  • The AutoType tiers on top: feed the synthetic positives to generate_autotype_negatives() for the structure-scramble (SP) near-misses that catch a mask checking characters but not placement.

This pairs directly with the mask-refinement loop in vignette("autotype-framework"): synthesize the positives, scramble them into negatives, score, tighten.

The round-trip connection

Rendering a canonical value out to a surface string is exactly what the formex format syntax does in reverse: each temporal ontology row carries a recipe for reading a raw value back to its stable ISO form (see vignette("formex")). A synthetic generator and a formex import recipe are two directions of the same format vocabulary, which is why a representation you can generate is also one you can stabilize.

When synthesis generalizes — and when it doesn’t

The temporal recipe — sample a canonical value, render deterministically — works for any family built the same way:

Synthesizable Why
temporal canonical instant + strftime rendering
coordinates canonical lat/lon + DMS / decimal / ISO-6709 rendering
checksummed identifiers (ISBN, ORCID, NPI) generate the body, compute the check digit
currency amounts sample a number + symbol/grouping/decimals rendering

It breaks down where values are defined by membership rather than by a rendering rule:

  • Names, cities, states — there is no formula for “a surname”; you need a gazetteer (see vignette("feature-engineering") on the lexicon features).
  • Free text (titles, descriptions) — no canonical value to render.

The test for whether to synthesize a family: can you write the value’s canonical form and a function that renders it? If yes, generate; if no, collect.
